beats.narration_text: BERT reads context beautifully — until you hand it an earnings call. I'm Anjana. Here's why financial language breaks a general-purpose model, and what it actually takes to fix it.

runningText 'reading the transcript…'
output lines resolve: 'same architecture, different training data' / 'every token sees every other token at once' / '10 milliseconds, three numbers out'

props.command: BERT is one of the most widely used language models in the world, but it gets confused by financial language — it reads 'narrow margin' as positive. Can you show me why general NLP fails on financial text, and what FinBERT actually changes to fix it?
output: every token sees every other token at once

beats.narration_text: BERT is one of the most widely used language models in the world. It reads text and understands context. But hand it an earnings call, and it gets confused. Financial language does not work like normal English.

show.event: 'BERT' lands center screen, bold; subtitle fades in — 'Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers' — then simplifies to 'A language model that reads context.'
test 1: 'The market reacted positively.' — green 'POSITIVE ✓' tag appears. Correct.
test 2: 'Revenue missed estimates by a narrow margin.' — tagged 'POSITIVE' again, red ✗ stamps over it. Wrong.
annotation lands: BERT read 'narrow margin' as positive — in finance, this sentence is cautious

props.sparkLine: Context isn't the problem. Finance is.

beats.narration_text: In everyday language, "exceeded expectations" is positive and "significant loss" is negative. Straightforward. But in finance, "beat estimates by a narrow margin" is cautious. "Headwinds" is not about weather. "Adjusted" usually means something was removed to make the numbers look better. The same words carry different weight when money is on the line.

show.event: pair 1: 'beat estimates by a narrow margin' — general (green) 'Positive! They beat it!' vs financial (amber) 'Cautious. Barely cleared the bar.'
pair 2: 'headwinds' — general (grey) 'Weather? Wind?' vs financial (red) 'Risk ahead. Challenges incoming.'
pair 3: 'adjusted results' — general (green) 'Improved!' vs financial (amber) 'Non-GAAP. Items were excluded.'
the gap between the two columns has visibly widened across all three pairs

props.sparkLine: The gap is bigger than you think.

beats.narration_text: FinBERT takes the original BERT model and fine-tunes it on fifty thousand financial sentences from earnings calls, analyst reports, and financial news. The architecture stays the same — the weights change. It learns that "decline" next to revenue is negative, but next to expenses is positive. It learns the difference between what words mean in general, and what they mean when money is involved.

show.event: simplified 3-layer network: embedding layer (bottom), transformer blocks (middle), classification head (top); label 'BERT' on the left
a stream of financial fragments flows up into the network — 'revenue growth,' 'margin pressure,' 'forward guidance,' 'operating leverage' — on 'fifty thousand financial sentences'
transformer blocks pulse, color shifts grey → warm gold; counter lands: '50,000 sentences'
box: 'revenue decline' → red arrow down → 'Negative'
box: 'expense decline' → green arrow up → 'Positive'; the word 'decline' highlighted between them — same word, opposite meaning
label glows and updates: 'BERT' → 'FinBERT'; on-screen-only caption: '"in line with expectations" → neutral, not positive'

beats.narration_text: Here is what happens when FinBERT reads a sentence. The text splits into tokens, each one becomes an embedding — a vector that captures its meaning. The transformer layers process these in parallel: every token attends to every other token at once, not left to right. The classification head outputs three probabilities. One sentence in, three numbers out, in about ten milliseconds.

show.event: sentence enters from the left: 'We expect moderate growth in the second half.'
the sentence breaks into 8 tokens, each a separate rounded block, arranging in a row
each token morphs into a vertical color-strip embedding; different words get different color patterns

attention web draws between every token pair; thick lines for strong connections ('moderate'↔'growth', 'expect'↔'second half'), thin for weak ones; caption: 'Bidirectional — every token sees every other token'
the web funnels into a classification head; three bars grow: Positive 0.24 (blue), Negative 0.11 (red), Neutral 0.65 (gold, glowing, longest)
a small stopwatch icon lands: '10ms'

beats.narration_text: Same architecture. Different training data. Different understanding. That is what happens when you teach BERT to read financial statements. It stops reading words. It starts reading money.

show.event: split screen: left 'BERT' (grey, generic document icon), right 'FinBERT' (gold, financial chart icon); transform arrow between them
left side fades to black — on 'stops reading words'
right side grows to fill the frame, warms — on 'starts reading money'
title lands: 'FinBERT' / 'BERT, Fine-Tuned for Finance'

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Same architecture as BERT — the weights are what changed. Fine-tuned on fifty thousand financial sentences. Attention lets every token see every other token, all at once. One sentence in, three probabilities out, in about ten milliseconds.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. "I use a general-purpose AI for a task in my field where the everyday meaning of a word and the specialized meaning genuinely diverge — the way 'narrow margin' means something different in finance than it does in conversation. Can you help me: one, list five phrases in my own field where that gap exists; two, tell me honestly whether the gap is wide enough that a general model would actually get it wrong; and three, if it is, sketch what a small fine-tuning or even just a better prompt would need to cover?" Paste that into Claude and find out if your own field has a narrow-margin problem hiding in it.
